item.title: Horible public key tricks:
item.description:
So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"

There is prior art of protest SSL implementations, but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be week, no one would know unless they actually try to break it.

A good protest should be obvious: 

# openssl s_client -connect maurycyz.com:443 < /dev/null 2> /dev/null \
    | sed -n /BEGIN/,/END/p | grep -zE '////.?*////' --color=yes

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----

ICN41m494GUBgwqYpAjLgdIubvyoJzBpACGuIl2QlJza1p/y
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.

The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent: 

# Encryption requires knowing e (public)
cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n

The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q. 

# Decryption requires knowing d (pivate)
= cyphertext^d mod n

= plaintext^e^d mod n
= plaintext^(e*d) mod n
= plaintext^1 mod n
= plaintext

Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.

The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.

My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.

The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product: 

58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176
(incrementing until the next prime...)
58174124 * 918491843 = 53432458367670532

As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.

From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key: 

# Single domain
openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request
certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request

# Wildcard
cat > config<<EOF
[ req ]
req_extensions = req_ext

[ req_ext ]
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[ alt_names ]
DNS.1 = *.example.com
DNS.2 = example.com
EOF
openssl req -new -key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request
certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request
... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.

The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.

Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) avalable charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice.

As for security, this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. I'm not aware of any factoring algorithms that could exploit key selection method, but I can't garantee they don't exist. The method may also produce a p and q that are close together, which makes it possible to easly factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also allow factorisation.

While I wouldn't trust these keys for anything important, they should be perfectly fine for serving a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires man-in-the-middle even if the private key is compromised.

Related:

  • https://tom7.org/httpv/httpv.pdf: [⭐ World's worst TLS server ]
  • /projects/badcert/gen.py: script to generate a vanity key
  • https://rya.nc/cert-tricks.html: More vanity certs
  • https://web.archive.org/web/20230305190629/https://ondergetekende.nl/vanity-rsa-public-key.html: SSH keys.

item.title: A bit about email
item.description:
Before you torch and pitchfork me, I'm aware most of this is simplified and doesn't go into edge cases, even though the internet is composed entirely of edge cases. Otherwise, I'd be writing a whole book.

First, some terminology; A typical email will past through many different components on the way to the recipient: 

1. Sender's MUA
[Via SMTP on port 465]
2. Sending MSA 
3. Sending MTA 
[Via SMTP on port 25]
4. Receiving MTA
5. Receiving LDA and message store
[Via IMAP]
7. Receiver's MUA

(These aren't all necessarily different machines or even different programs, but it is helpful to name each step.)

The mail user agent (MUA) runs on the user's computer and is what they use to send or read messages. Let's say they send something: that message will be uploaded to to the submission agent (MSA) which checks the user's password before handing off to the mail transfer agent (MTA).

The transfer agent's job is to talk to other mail servers and get the message to the receiving side's MTA. Once received, it's given to the local delivery agent (LDA) to be stored until the recipient checks their email. The name "LDA" is non-standard, but I use it to avoid having four different abbreviations differing by a single letter.

The reason for this structure is that when the system was being designed (around 1980), most organizations could only afford a single server. Maintenance was a full time job and updates often required multiple days of downtime. A well-connected computer might have dedicated single-digits megabit/second link that worked half the time.

This forced the MTA and MUA distinction: if the recipient's server isn't up when the email is set, the sending MTA will save the message and re-attempt delivery later. This way, short outages don't cause bounced mail. Since the mail client is an interactive program the user runs, a separate message store is needed to keep the email until it can be read.

Most MTAs are configured to continue retrying a message for five days, usually with exponential backoff: mine will wait 5 minutes after the first failure, and increase the interval to one hour in prolonged outages.

The MSA and LDA have always existed in some capacity, but have gotten a lot more complicated when people started accessing email from their own computers instead or remotely logging onto a server.

SMTP

Most communication happens over the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, including MTA-MTA delivery. To narrow it down a bit, I'll pretend do be an MTA sending email to blog@maurycyz.com.

The first step is to look up the receiving MTA for that domain: 

# dig MX maurycyz.com
[snip]
maurycyz.com.           300     IN      MX      1 smallcrow.com.
[snip]
# dig A smallcrow.com
[snip]
smallcrow.com.          300     IN      A       65.109.172.162
[snip]

Email is old enough to have it's own dedicated DNS record instead of using subdomain hacks or TXT abuse. The number is a priority (smaller is higher), which is used if multiple hosts are specified: a big email provider will have multiple servers to ensure timely delivery.

SMTP is a relatively straightforward text based protocol. The one catch is that most mail servers will require a CRLF as a data terminator. This can often be sent with ctrl-m, but using a tool that automatically inserts cartridge-return bytes is easier: 

# telnet
telnet> set crlf
Will send carriage returns as telnet <CR><LF>.
telnet> open smallcrow.com 25
Trying 65.109.172.162...
Connected to smallcrow.com.
Escape character is '^]'.
220 smallcrow.com ESMTP Postfix
HELO nowhere
250 smallcrow.com
MAIL FROM:<me@nowhere>
250 2.1.0 Ok
RCPT TO:<blog@maurycyz.com>
250 2.1.5 Ok
DATA
354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
From: <me@nowhere>
To: <blog@maurycyz.com>

Hello, world. 

.
250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as C870D7CD93
QUIT
221 2.0.0 Bye

Each line sent is a command, to which the remote server responds with a three digit number followed by a human readable explaintaion. 200 responses mean it worked, 300 is "carry on...", 400 indicates temporary errors which tell the sender to try again later, 500 errors indicate that the email should be returned as un-deliverable.

(If this seems similar to HTTP, that's no coincidence. A lot of the web, including its header syntax, was lifted from SMTP)

The first command is always HELO (or EHLO), followed the sending MTA's hostname. This is usually not the same hostname that's in an email address, but many providers require it to match the sender's IP address. . The next two, MAIL FROM and RCPT TO specify the address to deliver to, and the address for any failure notifications. Bounce messages are usually generated one step up from where the error occurred: in most cases the receiving MTA has a problem and sends an error code to the sending MTA, but by that time MSA has already disconnect, forcing an emailed notification. Those notification themselves use an empty MAIL FROM to avoid infinite loops.

Once the address has been specified and accepted, a DATA command is sent, followed by the actual message. This, at a minimum, contains the "From" and "To" headers along with some text. The message is terminated with a lone period to which the server replies to indicate that the message was sucessfuly handed off.

Final hop MTAs should forward the email to the LDA before sending back a status code. This ensures that they never accept a message which they can't deliver, which would result in a error notification. This "backscatter" message interacts badly with spammers that forge MAIL FROM: it turns their obviously bogus message into one that is likely to be delivered and cause a nusance.

There is no requirement for the addresses inside the email to match the ones in MAIL FROM and RCPT TO (also known as the envelope). The most common cause of this is a mail that has been forwarded. For example, a mailing list will set the envelope destination to match each member's email, but keep the original "From" and "To" headers intact so that replies work correctly. The envelope from will usually be changed to point to somewhere the list administrator will check for error notifications.

Now, it's not that intermediate systems don't modify the headers: Most stages will add a "received" header to record where they got the message.

While required for MTA to MTA communication, SMTP is used throughout the whole system. The mail client submits email using a different port, but over the same protocol. Communication between internal components (i.e. MTA to LDA) often uses the closely related Local Mail Transfer Protocol: the main difference is the assumption that the receiver doesn't have a message queue and will either deliver the mail immediately or return an error.

Submission usually uses TLS to port 465, with the addition of a password (in base64): 

AUTH PLAIN
334
AGh1bnRlcgBodW50ZXIy
235 2.7.0 Authentication successful

The one thing that's significantly different is the MUA's fetch, which operates on a "pull" basis. I won't go into the syntax here, but it's not terribly complicated.

... but if you actually try sending an email to, say, gmail, based on what I've written so far, it won't work. Some of that is due to them enforcing things like the Message-Id header: a unique identifier used to de-duplicate mail in cases where the receiving MTA accepts an email but the connection drops before the sender is informed about this. This causes the sender to try again later, which duplicating the message.

However, a big part of it is...

Authentication

Base SMTP trusts that every sender is be well behaved: anyone can send email as anyone else. In fact, many hosts were configured to accept and relay mail from anyone as a conveyance for when someone's usual server was down.

The original solution to bad behavior was to get the culprit kicked off the internet... but that fell apart quickly once the network grew and companies began getting involved: the first documented case of spam email was sent in 1978 and sold 13 million dollars in computers. While authentication doesn't prevent spam, it makes it possible to filter out unwanted senders.

Verifying sender addresses is not possible using the MX record, since there is no guarantee the same host is used for receiving and sending mail. The simplest solution is to publish the sending address in a seperate DNS record: 

@ TXT v=spf1 ip4:65.109.172.162 ip6:2a01:4f9:c011:841a:b01d::1 -all
; Roughly:
;   allow from 65.109.172.162
;   allow from 2a01:4f9:c011:841a:b01d::1
;   deny otherwise

However, that's not quite enough for the email empire. Big-tech also wants the email body to be signed with a cryptographic key published via a (DKIM) DNS record. This requires adding a step to sending mails, usually as a plugin for the MTA.

While I rag on big-tech a lot, but this is actually a sensible policy: SPF can only verify the MAIL FROM, since forwarding the email will chance the source IP address. DKIM signatures are attached to the message and can be used to verify the original sender (the "From" address) of a message, which is what's actually shown to the user in most cases.

However, both of these don't actually prevent spam, because spammers can just set up a few TXT records. Big-tech also requires the sender's HELO hostname to be consistent with their IP address, via both forward and reverse DNS. This helps prevent compromised devices from spewing out junk: a smart TV is unlikely to have a meaningful PTR record, and if it does, that hostname won't resolve back to it's address.

... unfortunately this policy also makes it impossible to directly send mail from most residential internet connections unless you own the address block. Of course, the solution is to pay a big-tech company money to relay your emails. If you don't like this, find a mail provider with more permissive rules: the only reason big-tech is able to keep their racket running that five or so companies control 99% of email.

The message

This is where SMTP stops being so simple. Let's look at the simplest possible email once it's been delivered: 

Return-Path: <alex@there>
Delivered-To: bob@here
Received: from here
        by here with LMTP
        id bs05E10S7Go4VQMAHrglgg
        (envelope-from <alex@there>)
        for <bob@here>; Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:21:33 +0000
DKIM-Filter: OpenDKIM Filter v2.11.0 here B05E67CD18
Received-SPF: None (mailfrom) identity=mailfrom; client-ip=313.33.33.337;
        helo=there; envelope-from=alex@there; receiver=here
Received: from there (unknown [313.33.333.337])
        by here (Postfix) with SMTP id B05E67CD18
        for <bob@here>; Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:20:42 +0000 (UTC)
From: alex@there
To: bob@here

Hello, World!

The format of the headers is superficially similar to HTTP headers, except that no line should exceed 78 bytes. (without the CRLF line terminator) Overlong headers are broken up and newly created lines are prefixed with whitespace to indicate that they are a continuation of the last header.

Mail software generally preppends headers to the start of a message, so it's helpful to read them backwards. "From" and "to" are fairly self explanatory. Next, the "received" header contains a note from the receiving MTA: it includes the source's HELO name, IP address, RCPT TO and a timestamp.

The MTA then performed SPF and DKIM checks, which came up empty: There's no signature and the MAIL FROM hostname is not publically resolvable.

The LDA added another "received" header, although it's not very helpful. More importantly, it tacked on the "return-path" with the original MAIL FROM address and recorded the mailbox the message was delivered to.

However, the body isn't always plain text. This is an email that includes formatting: 

[...]
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/alternative;
 boundary=----IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit

------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X
Content-Type: text/plain;
 charset=utf-8
Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

Hello, World! I can do bold text!

------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X
Content-Type: text/html;
 charset=utf-8
Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

<!DOCTYPE html><html><body><div dir=3D"auto">Hello, world! I can do <b>bold<=
/b> text</div></body></html>

------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X--

That's right, it's a web page!

However, since not all email clients can understand HTML, the message also includes a plain text version. This is done using MIME's "multipart" encoding, in this case, multipart/alternative, which indicates all the versions are functionally equivalent.

MIME's version number has been stuck at 1.0 since 1996.

The delimiter is a randomly chosen string, which allows multiple multiparts to be nested inside without escaping. Each section of the message has it's own headers, in this case, indicating that it's sent in the quoted-printable encoding. This allows the email message to contain any bytes without exposing the MTA to scary things like non-seven-bit ASCII: remember, the SMTP is 45 years old.

In quoted-printable, equal signs are used as the escape character: if followed by two hex digits, it decodes to that byte. If followed by a newline, both characters are removed. This is used to break long lines that could otherwise cause trouble.

In this email, "=3D" becomes a literal equal sign and both lines are joined together. If you've ever seen an email with stray equals or missing one or two characters ~ every 80 bytes, broken quoted-printable decoding is usually the culprit.

The second "content-transfer-encoding" is base64, which is used for binary files like attached images: 

MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr"
Content-Disposition: inline

--5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii
Content-Disposition: inline

Check out this file:

--5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="file.bin"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64

J7mtSdbQItOAi345nwaNkkTXrnDIRPA0DSwhbSAOwm2C/KoHjQIotY9lnJRMBRk9InQaHOxL
bb7DGd9EN6uRpjvCbox9xblAh3CxH7sl+YAkYcKw1V100RpBwMhgaXfUJBB3oRkLffgRwEyK
v9qFBLp9zZ+SiRJoRWbA4aZLexPhHZ35vFROVKYtiAeMlD1s15v3kPZvEADam0e45BoSaqmp
1S3z3b5wBIFHJUxQULD589MKaFx2Z2A+91pl/pbZWmZkzt55D/hZ05kjUUbXUnDnTYAQE2Gk
WnN+SnrQvfEO+Tz7AdrbLD1q2DgwWW+k0cVJLKjdwRxesGhAkQCZfHVrno6R4iXjTbInIbQv
hXzQiV840iUiUhk282WADd1ffJ0sot2Waf7XHLIE1lZVFQ3iGofYbw8pZlg3sb35AnIWPZKv
fbC6Yh95RV23R4K2NHeBX1rpl4bSSiftnD2RbsBzv7cgw/6M/Lj3O40NFGAaUC+J7TpAaXdi
tvlPsNQhMo8QRf/ub7WK42cPUlz1fKq1k1pzGN96YOsE5azMfF4vLANtbtbVmLIp2WmgBk0P
9IGMWy/xIAe0cOh+bqzru2+ojJGgx9uX4VSTP9BaTOwkVX5+rQfpp1qJodtHiO8sHw6Pg+Mg
WcpqQPC7118ccuT44cVpIRkwOSoJzsW++WM=

--5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr--

This is why size limits are often disappointing: the email will be 33% larger than the attached file. More efficient encodings (raw binary data) are supported by some MTAs, but may have to be converted to base64 somewhere down the path... which would break DKIM signing.

Generally:

  • No encoding ("7-bit") can be used if the message has short lines and fits in low-bit ASCII. However, "7-bit" is mostly seen as a null encoding for already encoded multipart containers.
  • Quoted-printable if the message is mostly text, but has something that risks breaking ancient software.
  • Base64 for binary data.

About TLS

The SSL/TLS used by mail clients is effectively the same as for a browser: the mail provider must go to a certificate authority, prove their identity and get a certificate.. Algorithms and ciphers are disabled at the slightest hint they may be insecure.

However, MTAs operates on "trusted" networks... although it's less that an attacker can't get access to internet traffic, but that if they could, it would be possible for them to pass an ACME challenge and take out a trusted certificate.

As a result, the goal is mostly to protect against passive eavesdropping: most sysadmins don't bother dealing with a CA and use self-signed certificates. (it's not like CAs have a good track record: 4)

Another weird thing about email is that MTAs don't use a separate TLS port. All connections on port 25 start as plaintext, then the sender issues a STARTTLS command and hands over the connection to a SSL/TLS library. It's somewhat janky, but it allows servers to attempt to use encryption and cleanly fall back if it's not supported.

Such an approach isn't great for submissions, since a fall back would leak the password... and baddies on shared networks or nosy residential ISPs can strip out the STARTTLS command. For this case, it's best to default use the dedicated SSL submission port: 465.

(This port actually has a bit of a history, with it being deprecated in favor of STARTTLS before being re-endorsed once we realized using optional SSL for passwords was a bad idea.)

So what??

Unless you write email related software or run infrastructure, most of this information is profoundly useless. However, there are a few things you might want to remember.

The underlying protocols allow five days for delivery, and it can sometimes take longer. Since users expect delivery in seconds and most emails are at least somewhat time sensitive, some MTAs are configured to send out delay notification if a message is taking a while.

You may want to find out if yours does this before assuming the recipient is ignoring you.

Emails are digital postcards.

A message will be stored and forwarded by multiple systems in plaintext. Anyone on the network path may be able to read your email: SSL/TLS is not universally supported and can trivially be stripped out by active attackers.

This is an inherent part of email: there's no way to tack-on strong encryption without breaking existing clients. If you need a guarantee of privacy, you must encrypt the message before sending, and the recipient must decrypt it themselves. Be careful with built-in tools like PGP: these generally make it way too easy to accidentally hit "reply-all" without encrypting, in addition to other flaws like exposing the subject line.

PGP stuff

Since publication, multiple people have written to me explaining how obfuscating the subject line (or warning if the user fills it out) is completly unreasonable to expect from a for a self-proclaimed privacy tool. At least in my eyes, "encrypted messaging" means encrypted, not 90% encrypted and 10% plaintext.

The lack of deniablity and forward secrecy can be excused as limitiations of email's store-and-forward architecture... but default plaintext and making no attempt to encrypt certain the subject line or attachments is a recipe for disaster: at least with vanilla email, people know it is not encrypted.

"Encrypted" email providers are largely snake oil. While the message store can encrypt messages and a custom MUA could decrypt them, the MTA must have access to plaintext. As a result, it provides minimal to no security against most attack vectors despite the "millitary grade encryption". The only way to fix email would be to get everyone to agree to switch to an end-to-end encrypted protocol... but the whole point of email is universal compatability: encrypted messaging can exist, but encrypted email is contradictory.

The best hope is to find a mail provider that can be trusted not to snoop messages. That is to say, not an Advertising company (google) or one that's been pushing hard for LLMs (microsoft / apple): both of these businesses create strong incentives to read your messages. Although you'll still have to hope whoever you are communicating with isn't beign snooped on by their provider.

Worse, DKIM signatures act as a lifelong proof that an email came from your provider's servers, even if a message is years old and has no clear chain of custody. This makes leaked, hacked, or snooped emails ideal extortion material: since the bad actor can trivially prove they haven't been fabricated.

This property, called non-repudiation, is generally not desirable for private messaging systems. Avoiding signing not an option if you want to interoperate with big-tech, but it is possible to regularly rotate and publish private keys. Before they key is published, the signature can be trusted to verify it is legitimate. However, once the key has been published, the signature can been forged by anyone and is rendered retroactively untrustworthy.

Since authentication is checked during delivery by the MTA and LDA, this doesn't affect how the email will be handled. However, it will cast doubt on the authenticity of leaked messages since the signature could have been forged with minimal effort.

While key rotation is common practice, most mail providers don't publish their old private keys, so the signature is still trustworthy (modulo the service being hacked). I would advise against emailing something you wouldn't be comfortable reading out in public.

Related:

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc821/: Original SMTP
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2045/: MIME extended message format
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7208/: SPF Authentication
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6376/: DKIM signing

item.title: Some thoughts on hosting email
item.description:
Generally speaking, email isn't as hard as its reputation would suggest. Yes, big-tech providers will occasionally send my messages to spam... but paying for commercial email doesn't guarantee delivery: emails within a single provider are generally safe, but in my experience, big-tech to other big-tech has a ~75% chance.

Because of this, having my own mail server is great for piece of mind: I can be sure that anyone can send me an email without it mysteriously vanishing. My reply might go to spam, but at that point we're already in communication and can sort it out.

A softer version of self hosting is to keep a big-tech account, but only use it for initiating conversations. Point the "reply-to" header at a server you run, and give that address when people ask for contact details.

Since replies to real emails never go to spam, this provides the best of both worlds: maximizing the chance that someone else will get your message, while also maximizing the chance that you will get theirs.

Receiving email requires:

  • A publicly routable IPv4 address
  • Any server: good uptime is not required.
  • A domain [optional]

Despite it being 2026, many mail servers still don't support IPv6: if you have a good ISP, it should be possible to get a public IPv4 address arranged. Otherwise, the only real option is to rent from a datacenter, which will cost some money.

(Note, there's no requirement for the VPS to actually run the mail daemon: It's possible to have it forwarding traffic to a box in your house)

The server itself doesn't have to be anything special. A "big" email is only a few megabytes, and people only send a few messages per day. However, disk space may be a consideration if you plan on having multiple users.

Mailer daemons will retry message delivery, and only give up after days of downtime. If it does, the sender will get a failure notification: emails will never be dropped silently.

Regarding domains, "ihavenoname@[65.109.172.162]" is a perfectly valid email address. However, doing this ties your identity to your hosting provider or ISP, which is not ideal.

Buying, or rather renting, a domain costs money. It's not a huge amount of money (around 1 $/month), but it is a significant commitment. If you let a domain lapse, someone else can buy it and take over your old address. I prefer to think of the cost as $800 per lifetime: not a prohibitive amount, but you should think twice before getting yet-another domain for a sideproject.

(Just remember that email needs an MX record)

Sending email requires:

  • An IP address with a PTR record
  • A domain

About IP reputation

Since a server can be spun up in seconds with nothing but a (possibly stolen) credit card number, spammers love VPS providers. Most hosting provider will put a stop to it once people complain, but by that point, the bad actor could have sent millions of messages, ruining the reputation of the rented IP address.

It's not uncommon for a provider to have some (or all) of its customer address pool blacklisted by big-tech email providers. Blacklists are often published, so this is something you can easly check. If only some address are soiled, it's often possible to delete and re-create the server until you get a clean one. Otherwise, you'll have to find a different provider.

Often, the best choices are the ones that block outgoing port 25 by default. Having to request access or satisfy account age thresholds is annoying, but this will help avoid problems with big-tech.

The domain is unavoidable here, because you'll need to make a few DNS records to prove the moral character of your packets. Specifically, you'll need SPF and DKIM. 

; SPF record
@ TXT "v=spf1 ip4:65.109.172.162 ip6:2a01:4f9:c011:841a::1 -all"

SPF tells receiving servers to accept mail from particular IP addresses and reject everything else. Importantly, this means if you have multiple different addresses, the mailer daemon will have to be configured to use a specific one.

Most servers will handle a missing SPF record as "deny everything", which is sensible: otherwise, even if someone had SPF at root, bad actors could spoof emails from a non-existent subdomains.

The second authentication mechanism is DKIM, which uses a cryptographic signing key published through DNS. Here's mine, but you will need to generate your own: 

2020._domainkey TXT "v=DKIM1;h=sha256;k=rsa;p=MIGfMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4GNADCBi
QKBgQDcysWHfXhdjsK3jWRnUKa3cdNF7gfl0EP/Xe2r5Ixqp7htPRVx7sntLgF1S5fODBM9o9xWSTwu
TuuFF0DLvkvi2fiddiSFa+0IXMb7sevhYIGha6Ewpk5h4vHkRIEGG7MDTlnXovgQpq5Q6MUymU6Z+Or
H6xXBaiwf8wOfZtRIYwIDAQAB"

Most providers also require reverse DNS on the origin IP address. This doesn't have to be the same domain as you are sending email from, but it should be a public hostname associated with your server.

If you want to improve your chances with big-tech, many of them allow you to register your domain with them:

  • https://substrate.office.com/ip-domain-management-snds/snds/jmrp
  • https://postmaster.google.com/

Both of these require an account with the same company.

Dealing with spam:

Spam hasn't been as much of a problem as I expected, despite my near-worst case setup: a catchall email and a contact address listed on a public website. All I've needed to deal with spam is:

  • SPF checking, but not enforcement. (default allow)
  • Light email obfuscation.
  • A blacklist of 12 domains and IP addresses

I'm not particularly worried about the spoofing potential of allowing unauthenticated messages since I have infinite addresses; If I get an email to my blog's comment box purporting to be a bill from my hosting provider, then I know it's fake regardless of what's in the "From" field or message body.

However, this relaxed SPF does still filter out a lot of the spam: most of the particularly obnoxious spammers forge emails from well known-domains which do have an SPF record.

There are lots of wacky solutions for email obfuscation: images, javascript initiated network requests, encryption, etc, etc. In practice, 99% of spam bots don't parse HTML and can be thrown off by something as simple as: 

<!-- A random comment -->
blog@maurycyz<!--.example-->.com

<!-- Or needless percent encoding -->
<a href=mailto:blog@%6daurycyz.com>email</a>

This works in every browser, is compatible with screen readers and not too hard to figure out by hand. More extreme measures would also work, but why bother?

With blacklists, there is a very long tail needed to get rid of all spam, but it doesn't take much at all to get it down to tolerable levels. For me, it was enough to block seven domains and five IP addresses (not address blocks) to get it down to around 3 messages per week: I think that's a sensible price for being sure nothing important will get caught up.

Security:

Getting your email compromised is bad. Not only does it have a lot of personal information, most services run password resets and account recovery over email.

Some attacks are technical, but many aren't: your server password should not be "password123". If you don't trust yourself to use a good password, set up key-based for authentication.

In terms of defending against exploits, the best thing to do is keep everything up to date and isolated:

Setup automatic updates and check back a moth later to make sure they work. Services should be run as separate unprivileged users: if your web server gets popped, the attacker should not be able to read your email.

One thing that is unique to email is just how aggressive people are be when blacklisting IPs: if your server gets used to send spam, good luck recovering any reputation. Because of this, it's a very good idea to lock down outgoing network traffic.

  • A web server doesn't need to make any outgoing connections.
  • A minecraft server needs HTTPS and DNS to authenticate users, but should not have access to anything else.
  • Only the mail daemon needs outgoing port 25 access.

(Also, make sure to lock down locally submitting email)

Reputation aside, this is good security practice. Remember log4shell, that trivially exploitable RCE against Java applications? It requires downloading a payload from the attacker's server, so proper firewalling makes it impossible to exploit. Additionally, almost all malware opens up a communication channel over the internet: a crypto miner needs to download the blockchain state, a stealer needs to upload the stolen data...

Also, specific to postfix with remote sumbission: while the mail server can verify that the connected user owns the envelope from address, it does not check the "From" inside the email which is all the recipient will see unless they dig into the headers.

Having two different addresses is intended behavoir. For example, an email recieved from a mailing list will often look like this: 

HELO somecorp
MAIL FROM: mailinglistbounce@somecorp
RCPT TO: me@me
DATA
From: fancytitle@somecorp
To: mailinglist@somecorp

Hello, world.

.

The envelope data provides instructions on how to deliver the message, while the headers inside the email retain what was originally sumbitted by the sender. This allows other features to work correctly: it would be goofy if replies were re-broadcast to the the list instead of going back to the original sender.

... but letting users do this at-will can get you in a bit of trouble: I recomend setting up a mail filter to ensure the two addresses are consistant before accepting a message.

item.title: The indicators of a quality website (somewhat silly)
item.description:
You know it's a good website when it:

  1. Uses subdomains (except for username.platform.com)
    ... especially multiple levels
  2. Has a non-standard port number in URL
  3. Is served over a plaintext connection
  4. Uses very nearly default styles
  5. All tag names are written in SCREAMING CASE
  6. The path ends in .html
  7. The URL has meaningful directories and names
  8. The HTML has typos
  9. Has commented out draft work

Of course, these are all just indicators of age.

1. The use of subdomains fell out of favor due to IP address exhaustion and reverse proxy software. If your going to be setting up a proxy anyways, it doesn't make much sense to fiddle around with DNS. (which often makes setting up TLS harder)

On my site, the server handling / and /mcu aren't even on the same continent.

At one point, it was standard practice to setup a subdomains per protocol in case one had to be moved to new infrastructure, but HTTP is the last one standing: public access FTP/Gopher/Telnet are just about extinct.

Even in places where they absolutely should be used, subdomains seem to have fallen out of fashion. Many companies will register a new domain for an internal service instead of putting it under their well known name.

The last surviving use is to isolate user provided content: any platform that allows custom HTML/JS/CSS will give each user a subdomain so that browsers know it's not from the main site.

2. Port numbers are another victim of reverse proxies. Additional services are likely to be proxied instead of being exposed directly, especially as they often rely on the proxy to implement rate limiting and blacklists.

Nowadays, it's standard practice to route everything through Cloudflare, which doesn't support port numbers in the URL. This is part due the huge amount of bot traffic from hacked IOT devices: please do not connect your TV/toaster/security camera to the internet.

3. Ciphered connections have been the default for a long time. Many hosting providers don't even offer plaintext as an option.

As a result, the old trick... 

# telnet maurycyz.com 80
Trying 65.109.172.162...
Connected to maurycyz.com.
Escape character is '^]'.
GET /misc/quality/indicators.html HTTP/1.0
Host: maurycyz.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Date: Mon, 05 Oct 2026 16:07:21 GMT
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 14891
[...]
Accept-Ranges: bytes

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang=en-us>
        <head>
        [...]
</html>
Connection closed by foreign host.

... likely won't work unless the site owner has gone out of their way to change the default to use a "less secure" configuration. (In practice, a hard redirect doesn't do much because an active attacker can just intercept it, and users are still protected from passive attackers because browsers use encryption by default)

4. Very early browsers didn't support CSS, and stylesheets were quite limited for the first few years. The resulting pages might have a custom background, but bear a strong resemblance to default styles.

5. All-caps tag names helps when reading printouts or using text editors that don't support syntax highlighting... both of which are very rare nowadays.

The rest (.html, meaningful paths, typos and comments) are indicators of handcrafted markup served from a directory.

While some antiquarians still do this, most webpages are published using a fully automated content management system: written in markdown (often by an LLM) and then stuffed into a chronological feed and newsletter. This lets people treat their website like social media, complete with inline ads.

Enjoying this post? Subscribe to the newsletter. Directly to your inbox.

You're lucky to get a hand written URL slug instead of: 

  https://someone.smallcrow.com/p/title-except-it-cuts-off-randomly

Put together, having most of these factors reliably dates a website to the 1991 - 1998 range, although many have been continually updated since.

However, age is a strong indicator of quality.

Keeping something on the web for decades requires active work, and in most cases, considerable expense. If someone thinks it's worth keeping around, it's probably worth reading.

... and you can be sure it's not LLM slop, which has caused a sharp decline in the quality of pages. Sure, it's spelled correctly, but its a rambling description of a reality that is quite different to our own.

Related:

  • /misc/domains/: The consequences of refusing to use subdomains

item.title: A rant about phishing: It's not the user's fault (and not DNS either)
item.description:
"For safety, don't click suspicious links"

Meanwhile, most organization's login flow redirects through: 

# This is a real example, but I've changed the names to avoid pointing fingers
https://www.[name of company].com/squawk/
https://login.[name of company].com/
https://login.smallcrow.com/324aa78a-03a6-66fc-23e1-4124fdsa213
https://experience.crow-cloud.com/[name of company]/auth
https://flock.auth.bird-security.com/authorization
https://api-deadbeef.bird-security.com/oauth/v1/authorize?token=DeAdBeEf
https://api2.bird-security.com/2fa
https://www.[name of company].com/cool/bird/
https://experience.crow-cloud.com/[name of company]/
https://www.[name of company].com/squawk/

Neither the username, password nor 2FA prompts are hosted on the company's own domain. Combine that with token expiration triggering random authetication pop-ups, it becomes nearly impossible to notice phishing... because the real thing looks identical to a scam:

All an attacker has to do is write a website with a password box and the company logo. The URL doesn't matter because users have learned to ignore it.

I'll admit that URLs aren't the most intuitive things, because the reading direction alternates. Hostname and scheme start specific and become more general, while the path is the other way around: 

https://funnies.maurycyz.com/memes/crow_hobbies.jpg
  |        |        |     |    |     |     
  |        |        |     |    |     |     (most significant)
  |        |        |     +------------ 1. Top level domain
  |        |        +------------------ 2. Operator
  |        +--------------------------- 3. Server name
  +------------------------------------ 4. Protocol
                               |     |
                               +-----|- 5. Directory 
                                     +- 6. Filename
                                           (least significant)

This URL is for crow_hobbies.jpg, located in the memes folder
of the HTTP daemon on the funnies server run by maurycyz.com

As a result, the important bit (the second level domain) is in the middle of the URL. This is something non-technical users must be taught: simply telling them to "avoid suspicious links" isn't enough.

However, the whole excersise is pointless if hostname isn't a reliable indicator.

For users to have any chance of spotting a scam...

An organization MUST use a single, well recognized, root domain. Internal services MUST be on subdomains of the root and MUST NOT use URLs like: 

# All these look like scams. Don't normalize scammyness!
https://[name of company]-auth.com/
https://[name of company].someone-else.com/
https://someone-else.com/[name of company]
https://auth.someone-else.com/[big UUID]

This is obviously important for login pages (since impersonating them would allow stealing credentials), but it SHOULD be applied everywhere to build good habits and prevent social engineering.

Links sent by email or SMS MUST be under the recognizable domain. If it's absolutely necessary to point users somewhere else, create a local redirect or link: 

https://[name of company].com/survey
->
https://crow-survey.com/[name of company].

This does not mean everything has to be hosted by the organization: many services allow bringing your own domain and links are free.

This rule also applies to phone numbers: do not send an SMS or email telling users to "call 0491-570-006", because there's no way to know if it's a scam. Contact details MUST be provided on a web page linked from the original message.

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119...

The hostname situation has gotten so bad that I've seen people arguing that it's a problem that subdomains exist, because it allows criminals to impersonate anyone they want with no oversight.

DNS is a hierarchical system who's structure hasn't changed in 40+ years:

There should absolutely no confusion over who runs any given website... except that it's standard practice to put great effort into making legitimate sites indistinguishable from scams.

(not even governments consistently use their assigned TLDs)

Related:

  • https://www.troyhunt.com/thanks-fedex-this-is-why-we-keep-getting-phished/
